# Worksheet: another reaction, and where the diffusion breaks

**~45 minutes**

The [chapter](../../chapters/05-stochastic-differential-equations.qmd) built the
chemical Langevin SIR model: the drift is the reaction propensities, and each
reaction contributes one column of noise. Here you keep that construction and
push on it twice. First you add a third reaction, waning immunity, which needs a
third noise column. Then you shrink the population until the approximation stops
being trustworthy, and see exactly how it fails.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there; not
reaching it is fine. Worked solutions are posted at the end of each
day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

## Greek letters you can copy

`\gamma` followed by `Tab` gives `γ` at a Julia prompt, but that completion
often does not fire inside a Quarto file like this one. Copy what you need
from here, or insert it from the command palette with the Unicode Latex
extension described in [Setting up](../../setup.qmd#optional-extras).

| Symbol | Reads as | At a Julia prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `β` | beta | `\beta` then `Tab` |
| `γ` | gamma | `\gamma` then `Tab` |
| `κ` | kappa | `\kappa` then `Tab` |
| `ω` | omega | `\omega` then `Tab` |
| `₀` | subscript zero | `\_0` then `Tab` |

A subscript is its own character too: `R₀` is `R` followed by `₀`.

Plain ASCII names work exactly as well if you prefer them.
:::

## Setup

This is the session's model, given so you can get straight to the new material.
Run it and check the peak looks familiar.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-setup
using CairoMakie
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using StochasticDiffEq
using StableRNGs
using Statistics
using Random

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

β = 0.05; c = 10.0; γ = 0.25; N = 1000.0
κ = β * c / N
u₀ = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
times = collect(0.0:0.1:60.0)   # fine output grid to limit missed-peak bias

function propensities(u, p)
    κ, γ = p
    S, I = max(u[1], 0.0), max(u[2], 0.0)
    return (κ * S * I, γ * I)
end

function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t)
    infection, recovery = propensities(u, p)
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - recovery
    du[3] = recovery
    return nothing
end

function sir_diffusion!(G, u, p, t)
    infection, recovery = propensities(u, p)
    G .= 0.0
    G[1, 1] = -sqrt(infection);  G[2, 1] = sqrt(infection)
    G[2, 2] = -sqrt(recovery);   G[3, 2] = sqrt(recovery)
    return nothing
end

# The session's `SDEProblem` call, wrapped so the rest of the worksheet is short.
# `reactions` is the number of independent Wiener processes, which is the number
# of columns in `noise_rate_prototype`.
function sde_path(drift!, diffusion!, u0, p, tmax, reactions;
                  seed = 1, saveat = 0.5)
    problem = SDEProblem(drift!, diffusion!, u0, (0.0, tmax), p;
                         noise_rate_prototype = zeros(length(u0), reactions))
    solution = solve(problem, LambaEM(); dt = 0.02, adaptive = false,
                     saveat = saveat, rng = StableRNG(seed))
    return Array(solution)
end

baseline = sde_path(sir_drift!, sir_diffusion!, u₀, (κ, γ), 60.0, 2; seed = 1)
println("peak infectious on this path: ", round(maximum(baseline[2, :]); digits = 1))
```

---

## Part A — waning immunity, a third reaction (~15 min)

In the session, recovery is permanent. For many infections it is not: immunity
fades and people return to the susceptible pool. That is a third reaction,

| reaction | who moves | propensity |
|---|---|---|
| infection | $S + I \to 2I$ | $\kappa S I$ |
| recovery | $I \to R$ | $\gamma I$ |
| waning | $R \to S$ | $\omega R$ |

so the drift gains a term and the diffusion gains a **third column**, one per
independent Wiener process. You supply the third propensity and that third
column.

You built this model yesterday, as a discrete-time map and then as a binomial
chain (the discrete-time worksheet, Part A). Same model, same $\omega$, same
endemic level. What changes here is only how the randomness is represented.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-a1
ω = 0.02                              # mean immune period 1/ω = 50 days
sirs_times = collect(0.0:0.5:400.0)

function sirs_propensities(u, p)
    κ, γ, ω = p
    S, I, R = max(u[1], 0.0), max(u[2], 0.0), max(u[3], 0.0)
    return (κ * S * I, γ * I, 0.0)    # TODO: replace the 0.0 with the waning rate
end

function sirs_drift!(du, u, p, t)
    infection, recovery, waning = sirs_propensities(u, p)
    du[1] = -infection + waning
    du[2] = infection - recovery
    du[3] = recovery - waning
    return nothing
end

function sirs_diffusion!(G, u, p, t)
    infection, recovery, waning = sirs_propensities(u, p)
    G .= 0.0
    G[1, 1] = -sqrt(infection);  G[2, 1] = sqrt(infection)
    G[2, 2] = -sqrt(recovery);   G[3, 2] = sqrt(recovery)
    # TODO: column 3 is the waning reaction, which moves people from R to S
    return nothing
end

sirs = sde_path(sirs_drift!, sirs_diffusion!, u₀, (κ, γ, ω), 400.0, 3;
                seed = 3, saveat = sirs_times)

G_test = zeros(3, 3)
sirs_diffusion!(G_test, [500.0, 80.0, 420.0], (κ, γ, ω), 0.0)

check("the waning reaction has a noise column", any(G_test[:, 3] .!= 0.0))
check("every noise column sums to zero",
      maximum(abs.(vec(sum(G_test; dims = 1)))) < 1e-12)
check("population conserved",
      maximum(abs.(vec(sum(sirs; dims = 1)) .- N)) < 1e-6)
check("susceptibles are replenished", sirs[1, end] > minimum(sirs[1, :]) + 50)
check("the infection is still around on day 400", sirs[2, end] > 10)

(; predicted_S = γ / κ, observed_S = round(mean(sirs[1, 401:end]); digits = 1),
   predicted_I = ω * (N - γ / κ) / (γ + ω),
   observed_I = round(mean(sirs[2, 401:end]); digits = 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

```julia
return (κ * S * I, γ * I, ω * R)
...
G[3, 3] = -sqrt(waning);     G[1, 3] = sqrt(waning)
```

The pattern is the same for every reaction: the column has $-\sqrt{a}$ in the
compartment people leave and $+\sqrt{a}$ in the one they enter, so the column
sums to zero and every Brownian increment conserves the population. Waning takes
people out of $R$ and puts them into $S$, which is why the minus sign is on row
3 this time.

If the conservation check fails, one of the two signs in the new column is
wrong. If the last two checks fail while conservation passes, the propensity is
still `0.0`, so the column is multiplied by nothing.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch05-sirs
#| fig-cap: "One SIRS path from the chemical Langevin approximation, with the deterministic drift for comparison."
sirs_ode = Array(solve(ODEProblem(sirs_drift!, u₀, (0.0, 400.0), (κ, γ, ω)),
                       Tsit5(); saveat = sirs_times))

fig = Figure(size = (760, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)")
lines!(ax, sirs_times, sirs[2, :]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2,
       label = "SDE")
lines!(ax, sirs_times, sirs_ode[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash,
       linewidth = 2, label = "drift only (ODE)")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### A1. Interpret

- The drift settles down to a steady level; the stochastic path does not. What
  keeps it moving, and why does that not fade away as the ODE oscillation does?
- Suppose you had given $S$, $I$ and $R$ one independent noise term each instead
  of one per reaction. Which of the checks above would fail, and why?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part B — how large must the population be? (~15 min)

The chemical Langevin equation replaces whole-number event counts by a Gaussian
with matching mean and variance. That is a good trade when events are frequent,
which is a statement about population size. Below, the same baseline epidemic is
run at three population sizes, with the initial state and $\kappa$ scaled so
that $R_0 = 2$ every time.

One thing to know before interpreting the output, because the code does not
announce it: the `max(u, 0.0)` guards in `propensities` decide what happens at an
empty compartment. Once a path steps to $I \le 0$, every rate becomes zero and it
stays there. That imitates extinction rather than modelling it, so treat the
fade-out counts below as qualitative. The exact jump process from this morning is
where a number would come from.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-b1
function summarise(population; seeds = 1:40)
    scale = population / 1000
    u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0] .* scale
    p = (β * c / population, γ)
    peaks, lowest = Float64[], Float64[]
    for s in seeds
        path = sde_path(sir_drift!, sir_diffusion!, u0, p, 60.0, 2; seed = s)
        push!(peaks, maximum(path[2, :]) / population)   # peak as a fraction of N
        push!(lowest, minimum(path))                     # most negative state, if any
    end
    return (; population,
            mean_peak = mean(peaks),
            relative_sd = std(peaks) / mean(peaks),
            deepest_negative = minimum(lowest),
            never_took_off = count(<(0.02), peaks) / length(peaks))
end

populations = Float64[]     # TODO: fill this list — try 10_000, 1000 and 100

results = [summarise(pop) for pop in populations]
for r in results
    println("N = ", Int(r.population),
            " | mean peak ", round(100 * r.mean_peak; digits = 1), "% of N",
            " | relative sd ", round(r.relative_sd; digits = 3),
            " | deepest negative ", round(r.deepest_negative; digits = 2),
            " | never took off ", round(100 * r.never_took_off; digits = 1), "%")
end

check("three populations tried", length(populations) == 3)
if length(results) == 3
    largest = results[argmax(populations)]
    smallest = results[argmin(populations)]
    check("fluctuations are relatively smaller in the large population",
          largest.relative_sd < smallest.relative_sd)
    check("the small population has runs that never take off",
          smallest.never_took_off > 0.2)
    check("the large population stays non-negative",
          largest.deepest_negative > -0.5)
end
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B

```julia
populations = [10_000.0, 1000.0, 100.0]
```

`10_000` is ten thousand: Julia ignores underscores inside numbers, and they are
there to be read. Each run takes a second or two, so all three together are
about a minute.

### B1. Interpret

- Between $N = 10{,}000$ and $N = 1000$, roughly how does the relative spread
  change when the population is divided by ten? The $\sqrt{a}$ in the diffusion
  is the reason; can you connect the two? Then check the same ratio between
  $N = 1000$ and $N = 100$: it is much larger. What is different about that
  case, and what does it tell you about where the scaling argument applies?
- Both smaller populations produce negative numbers of people, one or two of
  them, and at $N = 100$ a large share of runs never take off at all. One of
  those two behaviours is a genuine feature of small populations and the other
  is an artefact of the approximation. Which is which, and why is a deficit of
  two people a more serious matter at $N = 100$ than at $N = 1000$?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — three descriptions of one epidemic (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

You now have three models of the same baseline epidemic: this morning's exact
jump process, this afternoon's diffusion, and the ODE from Day 1. Here they are
compared on the distribution of the epidemic peak. The jump code is the session's
direct method, given again; you supply its propensities.

The peak is $\sup_t I(t)$, so it has to be read off carefully. The jump process
is taken over its events, where a path can only change; the SDE is saved on the
0.1-day grid above. A coarse output grid can step over a short-lived maximum and
quietly bias every peak downwards, which is a reporting artefact rather than a
difference between the models.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch05-c1
function gillespie(u0, p, tmax, propensities, stoichiometry, rng)
    u = collect(u0)
    t = 0.0
    ts, us = [t], [copy(u)]
    while true
        a = collect(propensities(u, p))
        a₀ = sum(a)
        a₀ == 0 && break
        t += randexp(rng) / a₀
        t > tmax && break
        target = rand(rng) * a₀
        j = something(findfirst(≥(target), cumsum(a)), length(a))
        u .+= stoichiometry[:, j]
        push!(ts, t); push!(us, copy(u))
    end
    return ts, us
end

# TODO: the same two propensities as the SDE drift, for state (S, I, R)
jump_propensities(u, p) = (0.0, 0.0)
jump_stoichiometry = [-1 0; 1 -1; 0 1]

jump_peaks, sde_peaks = Float64[], Float64[]
for s in 1:40
    ts, us = gillespie((990, 10, 0), (κ, γ), 60.0, jump_propensities,
                       jump_stoichiometry, StableRNG(1000 + s))
    push!(jump_peaks, maximum(state[2] for state in us))   # every event, no grid
    push!(sde_peaks,
          maximum(sde_path(sir_drift!, sir_diffusion!, u₀, (κ, γ), 60.0, 2;
                           seed = 2000 + s, saveat = times)[2, :]))
end

ode_peak = maximum(Array(solve(ODEProblem(sir_drift!, u₀, (0.0, 60.0), (κ, γ)),
                               Tsit5(); saveat = times))[2, :])

check("the jump model produced epidemics", mean(jump_peaks) > 50)
check("mean peaks agree within 10%",
      abs(mean(sde_peaks) - mean(jump_peaks)) / mean(jump_peaks) < 0.1)
check("spread of peaks agrees within 15%",
      abs(std(sde_peaks) - std(jump_peaks)) / std(jump_peaks) < 0.15)

(; ode_peak = round(ode_peak; digits = 1),
   jump_mean = round(mean(jump_peaks); digits = 1),
   jump_sd = round(std(jump_peaks); digits = 1),
   sde_mean = round(mean(sde_peaks); digits = 1),
   sde_sd = round(std(sde_peaks); digits = 1))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

```julia
jump_propensities(u, p) = (p[1] * u[1] * u[2], p[2] * u[2])
```

`p` arrives as the tuple `(κ, γ)`, so `p[1]` is `κ`. These are the same two
rates the drift uses; the difference between the two models is what is done with
them, not what they are.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch05-peaks
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the epidemic peak over 40 runs of the exact jump process and 40 of the diffusion, with the deterministic peak marked."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "peak infectious", ylabel = "runs")
edges = range(0, 260, length = 14)
hist!(ax, jump_peaks; bins = edges, color = (:firebrick, 0.5), label = "jump")
hist!(ax, sde_peaks; bins = edges, color = (:steelblue, 0.5), label = "SDE")
vlines!(ax, [ode_peak]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "ODE")
axislegend(ax; position = :lt)
fig
```

### C1. Interpret

- The two stochastic models agree closely on both the average peak and its
  spread. What would you have to change about the scenario to pull them apart?
- Both stochastic mean peaks sit above the deterministic one. The ODE is the
  large-population limit, so why is it not the average of the paths?

> *Your answer here.*
